stages.name: Liquidity trap
stages.title: Liquidity trap
stages.sub: Why cutting interest rates and using QE can stop working once rates are already near zero.

steps.q: A central bank has already cut its interest rate from 5% down to 0.25%. Is there much room left to cut it further to boost spending?
steps.hint: Think about how far a rate can fall below zero before it stops making sense.
steps.pre: So the rate is stuck at

steps.q: With interest rates at 0.25%, saving in a bank account pays almost nothing. If people expect prices or shares to fall, what might they do with their spare cash instead of spending or investing it?
steps.wrong: Spend it quickly before it loses value
steps.hint: If holding cash costs almost nothing in lost interest, and the future looks uncertain, what feels safest?

steps.q: During the 2008 crisis, central banks also created new money to buy bonds once rates were near zero. If nervous banks and firms just sit on this extra money rather than lending or spending it, does pumping in even more money keep boosting spending?
steps.right: No, the extra money stops boosting spending much
steps.wrong: Yes, more money always boosts spending by the same amount
steps.hint: What matters is not how much money exists, but whether it actually gets spent.

steps.q: Rates can barely fall further, and people are hoarding cash instead of spending it. Are interest rate cuts and QE still able to drive up spending in the economy?
steps.right: No, they lose their power to work
steps.wrong: Yes, they still work just as well
steps.hint: If cheaper borrowing does not tempt people to spend, and cash just sits idle, what has happened to the policy's grip on the economy?
